newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU demands Hong Kong elections within 12 months.
newsitem.headline: EU demands Hong Kong elections within 12 months.

text.p: The EU urged China on Thursday to hold elections in Hong Kong within 12 months, but said it was up to each EU country to decide whether to join a boycott of the swearing-in of the territory's new legislature, hand-picked by Beijing.
Foreign ministers from the 15-nation bloc unanimously agreed a statement calling on China to meet its pledge to hold elections at the latest within a year of the takover on July 1.

"If at any stage there appears to be any retreat by China on its commitment to bring in a new legislative council, we now have a basis for strong support throughout the European Union," British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook told reporters.

Cook said London had made no attempt at the meeting to persuade EU countries to join it in a ministerial boycott of the swearing-in ceremony of the appointed legislature, but he added that for a number it was "an open question".

He said he believed ministers from those countries -- whom he would not name -- would decide to skip the controversial event when they arrived in Hong Kong for other ceremonies and discovered what an important issue it was to Hong Kong's people.
"When these ministers meet the present legislature, I suspect it will help tilt the balance," he said.
Cook said the European Commission and the European Parliament had both decided not to send representatives to the swearing-in.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, who chaired Thursday's meeting, said all EU member states would be represented at the swearing-in but that it was up to each one to decide at what level the representation would be.
As for himself, van Mierlo said he would discuss the issue with the Dutch cabinet on Friday.
Despite media reports that London was lobbying its EU partners for a joint boycott, Cook said his intention at the Luxembourg meeting had been to get clear support for elections.

The statement issued by the ministers called for China to support continuing democracy in Hong Kong and to hold legislative elections as soon as possible and certainly no later than 12 months after the colony reverts to Beijing.
"We want to make sure that Hong Kong can boast a prosperous economy and also maintain its freedoms and liberties," Cook said.
Hong Kong democrats accused Britain and the Britain and the United States of easing their stance on boycotting the swearing-in by planning to send top officials to the ceremony.

Cook denied that Britain was taking a new position and rejected accusations that Europe was sending China a mixed message by having British ministers boycott the ceremony while their EU compatriots were present.
"I think there is a special duty on Britain and I am very content that Britain should be seen to take an advanced psoition because of our relations with Hong Kong," he said.
